title: Why is it raining inside my tent?
subtitle: The science of tent condensation

segments.narration: You wake up, and the inside of your tent is dripping wet. Did it leak overnight?
Probably not. That water didn't come in from outside. It came from you.
Over one night, a sleeping adult releases somewhere between half a liter and a full liter of water vapor, just from breathing and sweating.

props.label: Water vapor one person releases overnight
props.note: Roughly one or two water bottles

segments.narration: That vapor makes the air in your tent warm and humid. The warm air rises and hits the rainfly, which the night air has cooled down. Once the fabric drops below the air's dew point, the vapor turns back into water droplets.

props.heading: How condensation forms
steps: You breathe out warm, moist air
It rises and hits the cold fly
Below the dew point, it turns to water

segments.narration: The dew point is the temperature where water vapor starts turning into liquid. The more humid the air, the higher the dew point, and the easier it is to get condensation.
Calm, damp nights are the worst, especially near water with every door zipped shut. A light breeze, higher ground, and open vents make a huge difference.

So here's your checklist. Open the top vents. Keep the fly taut so it doesn't touch the inner tent. Skip low spots by rivers and lakes. Keep wet gear out of the inner tent. And wipe the fly dry before you pack it.
